docs.text: Introduction ¶ RuleSet is a data validation language that non-coding domain experts can use to develop, maintain, and communicate data validation rules. The accompanying data validation program, ruleset-engine , validates a data table against rules written in RuleSet. Key Features of RuleSet ¶ Atomic Rules — Each rule in RuleSet targets a single feature of your dataset. For instance, applying an "is not null" rule to a column will solely check for the presence of null values, without performing any type or format validations. Rule Stacking — You can specify multiple atomic rules for a data column. Rules are evaluated independently, and their order does not affect the outcome. A data column must pass all applicable rules to be considered valid. Successful validations are recorded with an "all OK" message in the log file. Rule Blocks — If a group of columns share the same rules, RuleSet allows you to define those rules once and apply them to the entire group. Rules that are specific to individual columns can still be defined separately. Conditional Validation — RuleSet supports conditional validations, which let you apply validation rules only when a condition is met. For example: if column A contains "John Doe," then column B must contain "1970-12-22." You may specify multiple consequent rules, e.g. if column country is "USA" then column State must be in ["CO", "NY", "FL"]; column Zip Code must be an integer and have 5 digits. No implicit evaluation — Data is never evaluated implicitly. All validation rules must be explicitly defined to be applied. No data modification — Data is never modified during the validation process. With these features, RuleSet lets you specify data validation rules at different levels of stringency — from a quick type check on every column, to fully conditional, cross-column business rules. The Rules File and Data File pages walk through a complete worked example.

docs.text: Data File ¶ The data file is the actual table being validated against your rules file. Accepted formats ¶ ruleset-engine accepts .csv , .tsv , and .xls / .xlsx format data files. Data files are expected to be tabular with column headers included in the first row. Example data file ¶ The table below ( top_15_squash_players.csv ) is what the rules file in Rules File validates against: Rank PSA_ID First_Name Last_Name Country Year_of_Birth Address Zip_Code 1 PSA9057 Mostafa Asal EGY 2001 18 High St, Alexandria 11574 2 PSA9086 Ali Farag EGY 1993 411 High St, Giza 11772 3 PSA6447 Diego Elias PER 2004 235 Oak Dr, Cusco 15441 4 PSA1932 Paul Coll NZL 1992 99 Beach Rd, Auckland 1010 5 PSA3884 Marwan ElShorbagy EGY 1993 55 Nile Ave, Cairo 11311 6 PSA7765 Tarek Momen EGY 1988 12 Lotus St, Maadi 11431 7 PSA8820 Victor Crouin FRA 1999 45 Rue de Lyon, Paris 75012 8 PSA1399 Joel Makin WAL 1994 73 Cardiff Rd, Newport NP10 8XG 9 PSA6233 Mazen Hesham EGY 1994 31 Zamalek St, Cairo 11211 10 PSA5431 Youssef Ibrahim EGY 1999 23 Freedom Rd, Alexandria 11432 11 PSA4738 Nicolas Mueller SUI 1989 90 Lake View, Zurich 8004 12 PSA3186 Saurav Ghosal IND 1986 77 Residency Rd, Kolkata 700025 13 PSA2567 Mohamed ElShorbagy ENG 1991 19 Queen's Walk, Bristol BS8 1SB 14 PSA9012 Baptiste Masotti FRA 1995 12 Place du Marché, Marseille 13001 15 PSA8777 Eain Yow Ng MAS 1998 38 Jalan Ampang, Kuala Lumpur 50450 Running ruleset-engine with this data file against the rules file produces a clean log, since every row satisfies every rule — see Log File for that output in full. Both the rules file and data file can be found in the examples folder. What happens if data file format is incorrect ¶ If ruleset-engine cannot read the data file at all — an unsupported file type, a corrupted file, or a path that doesn't resolve — it writes an error to the log file explaining what went wrong (e.g. Error: could not read data file. <underlying error> ) and exits without attempting any validation. It does not partially validate a file it couldn't fully parse, and it never modifies or attempts to repair the data file itself. This is distinct from a data file that parses successfully but fails individual rules (a wrong value type, a null in a required column, and so on) — those are reported per-column as validation errors in the log, not as a file-format error. See Log File for how each case is logged.

docs.text: Quick Start ¶ Install ¶ pip install ruleset-engine Run ¶ ruleset-engine --rules-file RULES_FILE --data-file DATA_FILE [--logfile-path LOGFILE_PATH] Required Arguments: - --rules-file RULES_FILE — Path to the file containing the data validation rules (see Rules File ). - --data-file DATA_FILE — Path to the data file to be validated (see Data File ). Optional Arguments: - --logfile-path LOGFILE_PATH — Directory path where the log file will be stored. If not specified, the current working directory is used. - -h , --help — Display the help message and exit. Notes: - Ensure the ruleset-engine command is on your system's PATH (a standard pip install handles this automatically). - Logfile names include a timestamp: YYYY_MM_DD_HH_MM_SS_ruleset.log . - See Log File for a full explanation of log output, with examples. A minimal end-to-end example ¶ ruleset-engine --rules-file squash_rules.ruleset --data-file top_15_squash_players.csv The Rules File and Data File pages build out exactly this squash_rules.ruleset / top_15_squash_players.csv pair in detail. Both files are available in the examples folder of RuleSet.

docs.text: Rules File ¶ A rules file is a plain-text file containing one or more RuleSet rules. It has no required file extension — .ruleset , .dsl , or no extension at all are all valid, since ruleset-engine only cares about the file's contents, not its name. Correct format ¶ Lines starting with // are comments and are ignored; comments may appear anywhere in the file. Every rules file must contain exactly one column names in [ … ] rule — this is the only required rule in RuleSet (see Column Rules ). Beyond that, rules are composed from the building blocks in RuleSet Syntax : global settings, column rules, value rules, rule blocks, and conditional rules — combined in that order. Rule order does not affect the validation outcome. Example ¶ Here's a complete, valid rules file. It validates a table of squash players- top15_squash_players_full.csv . Every column has a declared type, PSA_ID must be unique and start with 'PSA' , Country must be one of nine listed values, and a conditional rule handles the fact that UK postal codes (Wales, England) are alphanumeric while other countries' zip codes are numeric. Both the rules file and data file can be found in the examples folder. //Rules to validate top15_squash_players_full.csv and top15_squash_players_full_with_errors.csv. // Column ID should be unique, each value should start with 'PSA'; PSA0000 is not a valid value. // Column Country can have only one of the following values: //'EGY', 'PER', 'NZL', 'IND', 'MAS', 'WAL', 'ENG', 'FRA', 'SUI'. //Column Year_of_Birth should have the format YYYY //Conditional rules: //Zip for Wales should start with 'NP' //Zip for Egypt should be 5 characters long. //------------------------------------- column names in ['Rank', 'PSA_ID', 'First_Name', 'Last_Name', 'Country', 'Year_of_Birth', 'Address', 'Zip_Code'] all columns required no extra columns allowed column: 'Rank' description: "World ranking of the player. Must be a positive whole number." has value type integer is > 0 column: 'PSA_ID' description: "Unique player identifier. Must start with PSA; PSA0000 is not a valid value." has value type string is unique starts with 'PSA' is not 'PSA0000' column: 'First_Name' description: "First name of the player." has value type string column: 'Last_Name' description: "Last name of the player." has value type string column: 'Country' description: "Three-letter country code of the player. Must be one of the nine codes listed." has value type string is in ['EGY', 'PER', 'NZL', 'IND', 'MAS', 'WAL', 'ENG', 'FRA', 'SUI'] column: 'Year_of_Birth' description: "Four-digit year of birth, in YYYY format." has value type date-time has format YYYY column: 'Address' description: "Street address and city of the player." has value type string column: 'Zip_Code' description: "Postal code of the player's address. Must not be empty. Its type depends on Country; see the conditional rules below." is not null 'Country-Zip1' if column: 'Country' is in ['WAL', 'ENG'] then column: 'Zip_Code' has value type string 'Country-Zip2' if column: 'Country' is not in ['WAL', 'ENG'] then column: 'Zip_Code' has value type integer

docs.text: Column Rules ¶ Specify which columns must be included, whether all named columns are required, and whether extra columns are allowed. column names in [ … ] ¶ Description: (Required) List exactly which columns the table must contain. Syntax: column names in <list of column names> Example: column names in ['user_id', 'first_name', 'last_name', 'signup_date'] all columns required ¶ Description: Fail if any of the named columns is missing. Syntax & Example: all columns required no extra columns allowed ¶ Description: Fail if the data table contains any column not listed in the rules file. Syntax & Example: no extra columns allowed check column order ¶ Description: Physical column order must match the order listed in the rules file. Syntax & Example: check column order

docs.text: Conditional Validation ¶ Apply a rule only when a condition ( if ) is met. The if condition is a single column with a single atomic rule. The consequent ( then ) can include multiple columns, but each column can have only one atomic rule. Multiple if / then rules can be specified in one rules file. Each conditional rule needs a rule tag (a quoted string identifying it). Syntax: <Rule Tag> if column: <ColumnA> <ValueRuleA> then column: <ColumnB> <ValueRuleB> column: <ColumnC> <ValueRuleC> Example: 'USAStateZipRule' if column: 'country' is "USA" then column: 'zipcode' has pattern /^\d{5}(-\d{4})?$/ column: 'state' is in ['MD', 'NY', 'DE', 'VA'] One rule per column: Each column in the consequent takes exactly one atomic rule. A column block with two or more rules is not valid in a conditional rule: then column: 'zipcode' is not null has value type string To require several rules on the same column, write a separate conditional rule for each one and repeat the if condition: 'ZipRequired' if column: 'country' is "USA" then column: 'zipcode' is not null 'ZipIsString' if column: 'country' is "USA" then column: 'zipcode' has value type string The worked example in Rules File uses two conditional rules together ( Country-Zip1 and Country-Zip2 ) to apply different Zip_Code type rules depending on Country .
docs.title: Conditional Validation

docs.text: description: "…" ¶ Description: Attach a plain-language explanation to a column: block or a ruleblock: . Use it to record why the rules exist, such as the business reason or the source of a limit, so that anyone reading the rules file can follow the intent. The description is optional, and it does not change how data are validated. Syntax: column: <ColumnName> description: "<text>" <ValueRule1> <ValueRule2> ... ruleblock: [<ColumnName_1>, <ColumnName_2>...<ColumnName_n>] description: "<text>" <ValueRule1> ... Example: column: "Transaction_ID" description: "Unique identifier assigned by the payment system." has value type string is unique ruleblock: [ "First_Name", "Last_Name", "City" ] description: "Name and location fields entered by hand. Must be present and contain at least three characters." has value type string has min length 3 is required Usage notes Place description: immediately after the column name (or the ruleblock: column list), before any set tolerance at line or value rule. A column block still needs at least one value rule. A description on its own is not enough. The text can be wrapped in single or double quotes and can span several lines. Line breaks inside the quotes are kept as part of the text. Use double quotes if the text contains an apostrophe, for example "Don't leave blank" . An apostrophe inside a single-quoted string ends the string early and causes a syntax error. Make sure every opening quote has a closing quote. A missing closing quote makes the string run on to the next quote in the file, and the syntax error is then reported far from the real mistake. In this version of RuleSet a description: cannot be added to conditional rules. This will be included in a future version. A typed \n is not turned into a line break. Use an actual new line instead. Unlike a // comment, which the parser ignores, a description is part of the rule itself.

docs.text: Global Settings ¶ Global dataset settings that apply across the whole rules file (not to any one column). allowed null values in [ … ] ¶ Description: Treat the listed literals as null/missing values. Syntax: allowed null values in <list of literals to be treated as null> Example: allowed null values in ["Not Measured", "Not Collected", "Not Included", "-"] thousands separator is "…" ¶ Description: Specify the character used to separate thousands in numeric fields. Syntax: thousands separator is <seperator> Example: thousands separator is "." set tolerance at <NUMBER> ¶ Description: Specify the tolerance level used for numeric comparisons. The default is 0.001 — two values are considered equal if they differ by no more than that. Setting tolerance at this level applies it globally to all numeric comparisons in the rules file. You can also specify tolerance for an individual comparison (see Value Rules ); when both a global and a local tolerance are defined, the local tolerance takes precedence . Syntax: set tolerance at <tolerance level> Example: set tolerance at 0.00001 set tolerance at 1E-6 Understanding tolerance: In many real-world datasets, numeric values that should be equal differ slightly because of rounding, measurement error, or floating-point representation. RuleSet uses tolerance to determine whether two numbers are close enough to be treated as equal — two values are equal when the absolute difference between them is less than or equal to the specified tolerance: reference value │ ▼ ───────────────┬─────●─────┬─────────────── │ │ reference - t reference + t <------ tolerance ------> ▲ test value If the test value lies anywhere inside the interval, the comparison succeeds. abs(test - reference) <= tolerance ignore warnings ¶ Description: Suppress the warnings that value rules write to the log for null values and for non-numeric values in numeric comparisons. Errors are never suppressed. Syntax & Example: ignore warnings Warnings suppressed by this setting Warning message Reported by value … is null. has value type , has format , is == , is != , is > , is >= , is < , is <= value … is not numeric. is == , is != , is > , is >= , is < , is <= What does not change Errors are still reported. A numeric value that fails a comparison, or a non-null value of the wrong type, is logged as an error with or without this setting. is required , is not null and is null report violations as errors, so this setting does not hide them. Values listed in allowed null values in [ … ] count as null, so they are no longer warned about either. Rules that never produce null or non-numeric warnings (for example is in , starts with , has pattern ) behave the same with or without the setting.

docs.text: The Log File ¶ Every ruleset-engine run produces a log file (named YYYY_MM_DD_HH_MM_SS_ruleset.log ) with three levels of output: Info — Informational messages indicating successful operations and summary details: Confirmation of successful parsing of rules and data files. Summary statistics of the data table, including row and column counts, and counts of missing values. Notifications that all validation rules have passed without issues. Warning — Potential issues that don't halt execution but could affect validation accuracy: Columns listed in the rules file without associated value rules. Value rules defined for columns not included in the column list. Absence of any value rules in the rules file. docs.text: Rule Blocks ¶ If a group of columns share the same rules, RuleSet lets you define those rules once and apply them to the entire group, rather than repeating the same value rules under separate column: blocks. Multiple rule blocks may be specified in one rules file, and columns can still have additional rules defined individually elsewhere. Syntax: ruleblock: [<ColumnName_1>, <ColumnName_2>...<ColumnName_n>] <ValueRule1> <ValueRule2> ... Example: ruleblock: [ "First_Name", "Last_Name", "City" ] has value type string has min length 3 is required

docs.text: Value Rules ¶ Value rules are the building blocks of a RuleSet data quality schema. Each rule checks exactly one property of a column's values, and you combine rules to describe what valid data looks like for that column. A few ideas shape how they work: One rule, one check. Rules are atomic. is unique checks only uniqueness and has value type integer checks only the type. A rule never checks anything you didn't ask for, so each rule is easy to read, and a failure points to one clear cause. Stack rules to build up a schema. A column can have as many rules as you need, and every rule must pass for the column to be valid. Rules are evaluated independently, so their order does not matter. Develop the schema iteratively. Start with the checks you are sure about, often just a value type for each column. Run ruleset-engine , review the log file , and add rules as you learn more about the data. Columns that are listed in column names in [ … ] but have no value rules yet are flagged with a warning in the log, which gives you a running list of what is still unchecked. Change stringency one line at a time. To tighten a schema, add a rule. To loosen it, delete one. Because rules don't depend on each other, the rest of the schema is unaffected, and the same rules file can grow from a quick first-pass check into a strict specification. Nothing is implicit. Data is only checked by the rules you write, and it is never modified. For example, a first pass at a Rank column might only confirm the type: column: 'Rank' has value type integer Once you know the values should also be positive, add one line: column: 'Rank' has value type integer is > 0 To apply the same rules to several columns, use rule blocks . To apply rules only when another column has a particular value, use conditional validation . Block Syntax: column: <ColumnName> <ValueRule1> <ValueRule2> … Example: column: 'age' has value type integer is >= 0 is <= 120 Data Type & Format ¶ has value type <ValueType> has value type string Accepted value types: Value Type Description string Text-based data (e.g., names, addresses, categories). integer Whole numbers without decimal points (e.g., 1, 42, -10). floating point Decimal numbers (e.g., 3.14, -0.01, 2.718). boolean True/False values (e.g., true, false). date-time Date or timestamp values (e.g., 2023-12-25, 2025-03-27T14:00:00). See supported formats below. scientific Numbers expressed in scientific notation (e.g., 1.23e-4). complex Complex numbers with real and imaginary parts (e.g., 3+4j). has format <FormatType> has format YYYY-MM-DD Applies only to the date-time type. Supported date-time formats: [ HH:mm:ss , HH:mm , hh:mm:ss AM/PM , hh:mm AM/PM , HHmmss , YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss , YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss , YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm , YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm , DD/MM/YYYY HH:mm:ss , MM-DD-YYYY hh:mm:ss AM/PM , YYYY/MM/DD HH:mm:ss , YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.sssZ , YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss+hh:mm , YYYY-MM-DD , MM-DD-YYYY , DD-MM-YYYY , YYYY/MM/DD , MM/DD/YYYY , DD/MM/YYYY , YYYY.MM.DD , MM.DD.YYYY , DD.MM.YYYY , YYYYMMDD , YYYY ] Other formats for geolocation and currency data will be added in future. Presence & Uniqueness ¶ is required is required is unique is unique is null / is not null is null is not null Pattern & Membership ¶ has pattern /…/ has pattern /^[A-Z]{2}\d{4}$/ is in [ … ] / is not in [ … ] is in ['Active', 'Pending', 'Closed'] is not in ['Cancelled', 'Deleted'] Exact Value Comparisons ¶ is "<string>" / is not "<string>" is "USA" is not "N/A" is == <NUMBER> / is != <NUMBER> is == 100 is != 0 Numeric Bounds ¶ is > <NUMBER> / is < <NUMBER> is > 0 is < 100 is >= <NUMBER> / is <= <NUMBER> is >= 0 is <= 120 Local tolerance: is == , is != , and the bound comparisons above respect tolerance (see Global Settings for how tolerance works). You can set a tolerance local to one column's comparisons, which takes precedence over any specified global tolerance: set tolerance at 0.0000001 set tolerance at 1E-06 Length Constraints ¶ has length <INT> has length 5 has min length <INT> / has max length <INT> has min length 3 has max length 10 String Affixes & Substrings ¶ starts with "<string>" / ends with "<string>" starts with "ABC" ends with ".csv" includes "<string>" / does not include "<string>" includes "urgent" does not include "spam" Precision Rules ¶ has <INT> significant digits has 3 significant digits has <INT> decimal places has 2 decimal places
